brief: A herb planter of three cells side by side, each with a bin that drains.

requirements.evidence: Three full bases in a straight row: piece:-1,0,0, piece:0,0,0 and piece:1,0,0, joined by two joint bolts.

requirements.requirement: Each cell has a bin that drains
requirements.evidence: Each cell holds a full-depth drained bin (hex-bin-full-drain): 3 in total. Whether the plastic holds up to wet soil depends on the filament you print in; the configurator checks fit, not materials.

requirements.requirement: It is a herb planter: bins hold soil and herbs
requirements.evidence: All three bins are filled with soil and planted with basil (prop:1), parsley (prop:2) and thyme (prop:3).

finish.summary: I built the herb planter as a straight row of three cells. Each cell has a full-depth drained bin, filled with soil and planted: basil, parsley and thyme. All open faces are capped and the two joints between the cells are bolted together. The build check found no rule issues and no colliding parts (mesh check clear). There are 20 parts, about 1.55 kg of filament and roughly 37 hours of printing. The plants and soil are only there to show what it's for; they aren't on the parts list.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
